title: Montaigne close
hookLine: weeks with a man who wrote about himself and found everyone

lines: A TOWER, A DESK, A RUNAWAY MIND.
A CAT, A HORSE, A KIDNEY STONE.
cards: A round tower. Sayings painted on the ceiling beams. A man at a desk, writing down what his runaway mind does when it's left alone.

Since then: a cat who might be playing with him, a fall from a horse that felt softer than he feared, a kidney stone, a mayor who was never quite the same person as Montaigne, and a philosopher who sits on his own bottom like everyone else.
He set out to write only about himself, and somehow readers keep finding themselves in it. Today the book closes.

teach.b: First, the name. Montaigne called his chapters essais, which in his French means trials, tries, attempts. Not conclusions.
He was trying out his judgment on whatever was in front of him, a cannibal, a cat, a cough, and watching what it did. Second, the strange result. He says he himself is the matter of his book.

teach.h: ONE LIFE, THE WHOLE HUMAN CONDITION.
teach.b: Yet he also says every person carries the whole form of the human condition. So by looking honestly at one ordinary life, his own, he was looking at everyone's. That's why a reader can open him at random and feel caught.
Third, he didn't call it finished.

teach.h: HE KEPT ADDING IN THE MARGINS.
teach.b: Even after the Essays were printed, he kept adding in the margins, putting a second thought beside the first without striking the first out. Fourth, the people who came after.
Tomorrow this path turns to Ralph Waldo Emerson, an American writer who read Montaigne closely and wrote an essay about him.

teach.h: CUT THESE WORDS, AND THEY WOULD BLEED.
teach.b: Of the Essays, Emerson said: "Cut these words, and they would bleed; they are vascular and alive." Not a system to obey, but a living voice that keeps trying.
Here are a few of the lines carried through this block: my tower, the runaway horse, what do I know, who's playing whom, my own bottom, haven't I lived, ordinary pleasures, keep curious.
And one more, the one Montaigne would hand you: not his attempt, but yours.

how: People who love Montaigne often keep a notebook of short, honest pieces about their own lives, written as attempts rather than finished arguments, sometimes adding to old entries years later.

o: the last day with Montaigne, whose essays were tries
the final ruling Montaigne gave on how to live
the lock Montaigne put on his tower library door

games.q: the Montaigne block: tap the pairs.

s: Montaigne finished the Essays and never touched them again
he kept adding in the margins, putting second thoughts beside first ones.
he says every person carries the whole form of the human condition
so looking at one ordinary life meant looking at everyone's.
Emerson called Montaigne's words vascular and alive
"cut these words, and they would bleed."

games.q: you've written a page about yourself and it isn't finished. what would Montaigne do?
o: throw it away until it's perfect.
keep it, and add to it in the margins.
turn it into a rule for others.
games.why: he kept his essays open to the end, adding second thoughts beside the first. an attempt stays an attempt.

practice: Write a short essay of your own, a few sentences on paper, on your phone, or just in your head, about something small from your life: how you sleep, a friend, a fear, a habit you can't explain.
Begin the way Montaigne might, here is what I notice about it, then add one honest sentence you wouldn't usually say out loud. Don't polish it; it's an attempt.

wordCard.voice: Montaigne close. The end of our block on a man who tried out his judgment on his own life, and in it found the whole human condition. Today's word.

orig.note: Montaigne's French title (in Latin letters): trials, tries, attempts.

carryVoice: Your line: my attempt. A rough try is worth keeping and adding to. Montaigne's block, done.
